operationalization: Place foraminifera, radiolaria and ciliates in a morphospace and on phylogenies built from molecular sequences. Repeated origin of the same simple forms in lineages that those sequences separate would support the claim; form-twins that are consistently monophyletic once characters are few would weigh against it.

candidate_datasets.name: mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Image-backed taxonomy of foraminifera and radiolaria through geological time, for comparing shared simple forms across ages and places

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public nucleotide sequences for phylogenies that do not assume the morphological groups under test

candidate_datasets.name: Endless Forams
candidate_datasets.role: Tens of thousands of identified modern planktonic foraminiferal images for within- and between-species shape overlap

obstacles: Soft-bodied infusoria lack a fossil record, so the deep-time half of the claim is testable mainly for mineralized skeletons.
Taxonomic practice still splits some of these groups by the same simple outlines the claim says are physically forced.
rationale: Molecular trees and large image libraries can show whether identical simple tests recur in distant lineages, which is the genealogical content of the claim. The further assertion that a physical force produced those forms is not a variable in these archives, and ciliates are far more thinly covered than planktonic foraminifera. A full refutation across minute organisms and geological time would need a compilation the present databases only partly support.

operationalization: Fit Lagena tests to a surface of revolution and compare that symmetry class with any records of orientation during calcification. Unduloids formed while the axis is vertical, and winged tests formed while it is horizontal, would support the claim; the reverse pairing would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: bforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated deep-sea benthic foraminifera, including Lagena, for scoring rotational symmetry against bilateral flattening

candidate_datasets.name: foraminifera.eu
candidate_datasets.role: Photograph collection of foraminiferal tests, including Lagena, for the same shape comparison

obstacles: Public images record finished tests, not the posture of the living cell while the shell was secreted.
An unduloid of revolution is also the expected outcome of any axisymmetric growth rule, so shape alone does not identify a hanging-drop posture.
rationale: Shell archives are good enough to test whether flask-shaped Lagena are surfaces of revolution and winged forms are not. The claim itself is about orientation during formation, and that life-position variable is not in those collections. Shape is a usable proxy with a serious confound, so only part of the claim can be resolved now.

operationalization: On Lagena and similar elongated vesicles, measure wall thickness relative to local diameter and the direction of folds. Longitudinal flutes on thin, strongly curved regions and transverse pleats on thick narrow necks would support the claim; the opposite pattern, or no association, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: bforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Published illustrations of Lagena, some showing longitudinal costae and annular neck ornament, for a first pass at fold direction

candidate_datasets.name: foraminifera.eu
candidate_datasets.role: Additional Lagena photographs covering flask, fluted and winged tests

obstacles: Most catalog images do not report wall thickness, so the stiffness variable has to be inferred or measured from a subset of sections and micro-CT.
Genetic ornament can imitate mechanical wrinkles, and hydroid gonangia are not in the foraminiferal archives.
rationale: Fold direction and chamber proportions are visible on existing Lagena plates, and the predicted switch from longitudinal to transverse folds is a sharp pattern. Thickness, the variable that is supposed to cause the switch, is only sporadically available, and the non-foraminiferal cases in the claim are uncompiled. The association can be tested for Lagena more readily than for the full scope.

operationalization: Measure axopod angles to the cell surface and the spacing of surface depressions, and compare that geometry with the ultrastructure of the filament. Radial filaments normal to the surface would match the stated outcome; filaments positioned by an internal axoneme, or oblique filaments with the same surface film, would count against surface-tension pull as the placing mechanism.
obstacles: Heliozoan electron micrographs and live orientations are scattered through papers rather than gathered in one public morphometric table.
A radial arrangement is expected under several cytoskeletal rules, so static angles do not isolate symmetrical surface-tension pull.
rationale: The geometric half, radial filaments and honeycomb depressions, is measurable wherever Actinophrys-type cells have been imaged in three dimensions. Public coverage is a handful of classical and modern studies, not a downloadable survey of heliozoa and radiolarian axopodia. Distinguishing a surface-film tug from microtubule anchoring needs those ultrastructures, which exist only piecemeal.

operationalization: Segment the trypanosome undulating membrane in three-dimensional electron microscopy and test whether its surface has constant mean curvature and lacks internal cytoplasm and cytoskeleton. A naked film whose waves persist without flagellar bending would support the claim; a cytoplasmic fold waved by the flagellar apparatus would refute the soap-film account.

candidate_datasets.name: EMDB EMD-23621
candidate_datasets.role: Public cryo-electron tomogram of the bloodstream-form Trypanosoma brucei flagellum, for testing whether the flagellum-associated membrane is a structured fold or an empty film

candidate_datasets.name: Electron Microscopy Data Bank
candidate_datasets.role: Further public trypanosome flagellar maps, including axoneme and paraflagellar-rod averages

obstacles: Available tomograms center on the axoneme and paraflagellar rod, so the mean curvature of the whole undulating membrane is only partly in frame.
Trichomonas and spermatozoa with undulating membranes are outside this trypanosome archive, and static maps do not show whether the wave is actively driven.
rationale: Open trypanosome tomograms can decide whether the membrane along the flagellum is an empty film or a fold built on an axoneme. That resolves the structural core for Trypanosoma brucei and leaves the developmental story, the constancy of mean curvature, and the denial of active motility only partly tested. Related flagellates in the stated scope are not in the same deposits.

operationalization: Compute mean curvature over reconstructed mammalian red-cell surfaces and compare discocytes with cells that have rounded in hypotonic or spherocytogenic conditions. Constant mean curvature on the biconcave disc would refute the claim; curvature that varies over the disc, together with a shift toward a sphere when the medium is diluted, would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Simionato red blood cell confocal library
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D confocal stacks of human red cells, including discocytes and spherocytes, for mean-curvature measurement

obstacles: The library is human-dominated, so non-mammalian vertebrate corpuscles in the stated scope are thinly covered.
Its spherocytes are not a controlled dilution series, so the hypotonic-sphering clause needs a separate public experiment.
rationale: Biconcave geometry maps directly onto surface curvature, and a large open set of three-dimensional red-cell reconstructions contains the shapes required. A small team can test constant versus varying mean curvature with standard surface analysis. The hedged suggestion of osmotic or fluid-crystal forces is broader than the curvature test, but the negative claim that the corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure is decidable now.

operationalization: Place decapod sperm in a graded osmotic series and in equiosmolar salts of different molecular weight, and record the shape sequence from the sphere. Support would be a single shrinkage pathway ordered by osmolarity, with matching shapes at molecular-weight-proportional concentrations; stable species-specific shapes across that series would refute the claim.
obstacles: No public osmotic series exists for the named genera Inachus, Galathea, Dromia and crayfish.
Isolated micrographs of crustacean sperm lack the paired external concentration and surface-area measurements the test needs.
rationale: The claim states a clear experimental pattern: normal sperm shape is one frame of an osmotic shrinkage sequence, and equivalent osmolarities match. That pattern would discriminate osmotic collapse from a fixed cytoskeletal mould. The required concentration series is not in a public dataset, so the test cannot be run on existing downloads.

operationalization: Map intracellular fibrils onto the spiral or other non-equilibrium outline of decapod sperm and ciliates, and ask whether the outline relaxes when those fibrils are absent. A fibrillar scaffold whose geometry matches the departure from a surface-tension figure would support the claim; the same outlines without such fibrils, or fibrils that do not follow the spiral, would weaken it.
obstacles: Cortex and sperm ultrastructure are spread across individual papers, with quantitative shape-versus-fibril tables for only a few model ciliates.
Nearly all of these cells have a cytoskeleton, so presence alone does not show that the fibrils act as Plateau frames.
rationale: Electron microscopy of Paramecium, Tetrahymena and some crustacean sperm can test whether odd outlines are braced by fibrils. The mechanical claim, that those fibrils are elastic restraints equivalent to Plateau's wires, needs perturbation or stiffness data that are not archived for the stated groups. Existing images therefore cover a structural proxy for a few species.

operationalization: Track where wall or membrane material first accumulates and whether that accumulation follows surface activity, as the Gibbs adsorption rule requires, or arrives by vesicular delivery. Accumulation of tension-lowering constituents at a free surface without exocytosis would support the claim; wall polymers delivered by vesicles on a biosynthetic timetable would refute the strong adsorption-only reading.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public confocal and electron-microscopy studies of plant, fungal and animal membrane and cell-wall assembly

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Additional open bioimage collections of secretion and cell-surface deposition

obstacles: These archives record trafficking and localization far more often than surface tension or adsorbability of the deposited molecules.
Blood-corpuscle membranes and protozoan cyst walls are poorly represented relative to model plant and fungal walls.
rationale: Open imaging can test the strong claim that a wall is nothing more than equilibrium adsorption, because vesicular delivery is visible in well-studied cells. The Gibbs-Thomson premise itself, that the accumulated molecules are there because they lower surface tension, is not a field in those image sets. Model plants and yeasts are adequate; the full scope across protozoa and corpuscles is not.

operationalization: In sponges and radiolaria, record whether mineral is laid down on cell or vacuole boundaries and whether spicule geometry follows those boundaries. Systematic siting on interfaces, with spicule branches tracking junction lines, would support the claim; intracellular initiation away from boundaries would refute it.
obstacles: Isolated-spicule collections omit the cells and vacuoles whose boundaries are the claimed template.
A static section cannot tell whether the boundary preceded the spicule or formed around it.
rationale: Interface siting is directly visible in histological and electron-microscopic series, and those series exist for a number of sponges and some radiolaria. They are scattered in papers rather than released as a single open table of spicule position against cell boundaries. The geometric association can be remeasured for the illustrated species, with the temporal-order confound left open.

operationalization: Compare encystment or wall deposition in amoeboid and plasmodial protists while the cell is still a creeping film with the same events after it has rounded. Cysts or walls forming only on rounded cells would support the claim; membranes secreted by still-flattened or streaming protoplasm would refute it.
obstacles: Time-lapse of encystment is public for a few species such as Acanthamoeba and Dictyostelium, not for amoeboid protists generally.
Rounding and encystment can be co-triggered by a developmental switch, so their coincidence does not isolate positive surface tension as the requirement.
rationale: The observable pattern, no cyst on a creeping film and a cyst after rounding, is recorded for several laboratory protists. Direct surface-tension measurements are almost never paired with those films. Existing observations can check the morphological sequence in a small subset and cannot separate the tension mechanism from other encystment programs.

operationalization: Test whether encystment and resting-egg shell thickening track falling temperature after photoperiod, crowding and food are accounted for, and whether wall-material adsorption rises as temperature falls. A temperature-specific increase in adsorption and encystment would support the claim; encystment timed by photoperiod at constant temperature would weaken it.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Public environmental and biological records, including microfossil cyst occurrences that can be aligned with temperature, as a weak proxy for the seasonal timing half of the claim

obstacles: Resting-egg and cyst induction is confounded with photoperiod and resource cues that field temperature series do not separate.
Adsorbability of the actual wall molecules versus temperature is laboratory physical chemistry and is not in these environmental archives.
rationale: Seasonal encystment and winter-egg formation are documented for rotifers, cladocerans and some protists, so the ecological association can be inspected for a subset. The claimed mechanism, reduced temperature favouring adsorption, is not what those datasets measure. Photoperiod and crowding remain serious alternative drivers, which keeps the test only partly informative.

operationalization: Ask whether mitochondria are bounded organelles with a characteristic proteome and functions, or unstructured clumps of mixed cytoplasm drawn to a cell pole. A double membrane, a mitochondrial proteome and a distributed network would refute the clump account; granules with no specific composition, gathered and drawn out with the cell axis, would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: MitoCarta3.0
candidate_datasets.role: Inventory of mammalian mitochondrial proteins, sub-compartments and pathways, used to test whether these bodies have a specific identity

candidate_datasets.name: Human Protein Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Subcellular images showing mitochondrial localization across human cell types named in the claim

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Cell Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional images of mitochondria in human cells, for testing whether they are polar clumps or a distributed organelle network

obstacles: The same resources do not cover every non-mitochondrial fibril the wording also includes.
Mammalian cultured cells dominate the image sets relative to germ cells and invertebrate tissues.
rationale: The claim denies that mitochondria and similar granules are special entities and treats them as surface-tension clumps. Open proteomes and image volumes show membrane-bounded organelles with pathway annotations and a cell-wide distribution, which is a direct and standard test of that denial. A counterexample of this clarity resolves the universal claim even though some minor fibrillar inclusions remain less studied.

operationalization: Co-register local potassium at the cell surface with an independent measure of local surface tension. Potassium enriched where tension is independently low, and inorganic salts shown to raise the relevant interfacial tension, would support the claim; potassium patterns that ignore measured tension, or tension inferred only from the potassium map, would not test it.
obstacles: Modern potassium imaging rarely shares a coordinate frame with a surface-tension measurement.
Using the potassium map itself as the tension map makes the test circular.
rationale: The claim links two variables, potassium localization and local surface tension, by the physicochemical rule that these salts raise tension and therefore collect where tension is weak. Historical cobalt-nitrite plates and scattered elemental maps give the potassium side only. Without paired tension data the indicated mechanism cannot be confirmed or refuted from public datasets.

operationalization: Map potassium through conjugation in zygnematacean filaments and through rhizoid outgrowth of Equisetum spores. A potassium peak that precedes the bulge and disperses when symmetry returns would support the claim; outgrowths without a potassium peak, or peaks that persist after the cell is symmetrical, would refute it.
obstacles: The spatial potassium records for Pleurocarpus, Mesocarpus and Equisetum spores are essentially early histochemical plates, not reusable measurements.
A spatial coincidence, even if remeasured, would still leave open whether potassium causes the bulge or follows local growth.
rationale: Coincidence of a potassium peak with the conjugation papilla or the spore outgrowth is a concrete spatial prediction. No current public dataset repeats that histochemistry with coordinates and time. The test is straightforward in principle and cannot be run on data that exist today.

operationalization: Quantify potassium within a defined distance of ciliary and flagellar bases in ciliates and flagellates, and compare that zone with the rest of the cortex. A repeated basal enrichment, lined up with the basal ridge or flagellar protuberance, would support the empirical claim; a flat cortical potassium field would refute it.
obstacles: Elemental or indicator maps of Vorticella and monads are not deposited as a reusable public set.
Basal bodies concentrate many ions and proteins, so a potassium peak would not by itself establish weakened surface tension.
rationale: Basal potassium enrichment is a local, measurable pattern, and the morphological ridge at a ciliary row is visible in existing micrographs. The potassium half of the observation is not available as open, spatially registered data for the stated cells. Reanalysis of published plates would not replace a modern survey.

operationalization: For unicells with a measured asymmetry, test whether the outline matches a surface whose local curvature corresponds to a localized change in surface tension, against a cytoskeletal template that survives membrane extraction. A curvature field that accounts for the asymmetry, and that disappears when cortical mechanics are altered, would support the claim; asymmetries that persist as patterned cytoskeleton with no curvature match would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Large public image sets of mineralized unicells whose departures from symmetry can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Reviewed cell images, including protists, for comparing cortical ultrastructure with outline asymmetry

obstacles: Almost any outline can be assigned a local tension after the fact, so a mere correlation is a weak decision rule.
Tension is rarely measured on the same cells whose shapes fill the taxonomic image libraries.
rationale: Image archives cover a wide range of unicellular outlines, so a restricted geometric reading can be tried on mineralized and a few imaged protists. The claim that those departures from symmetry are produced by local surface tension does not specify a result that would rule out other cortical forces. That gap in discriminating power, not a lack of photographs, is what keeps the claim only partly testable.

operationalization: In segmented cell aggregates, compare wall areas and junction angles with the minimal-area surfaces expected for the observed cell volumes. Agreement with minimal-area geometry would support the geometric half; systematic excess area or a different angle rule would refute it, while an independent tension measurement would be required to credit surface tension rather than another minimizing agency.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D confocal stacks and expert segmentations of shoot apical meristems for junction angles and cell-face areas

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: About 100 confocal volumes of early embryos with cell walls stained, for aggregate geometry from the one-cell stage onward

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public epithelial and other tissue volumes in which cell-contact surfaces can be measured

obstacles: Minimal-area packing is also predicted by adhesion energy and cortical contractility, which these images do not separate from surface tension.
Plant meristems and a few animal epithelia stand in for tissues in general.
rationale: Segmented tissues already in public archives are enough to test whether cell aggregates approximate surfaces of relatively minimal area. That is the measurable pattern the claim predicts. Naming surface tension as the agency needs a force measurement these datasets do not contain, so the geometric half is testable and the causal half remains confounded.

operationalization: Classify plant-cell junctions by whether the older wall was already rigid when the new partition met it, and measure the angle. Right angles confined to rigid-wall meetings, with fluid-fluid meetings near 120 degrees, would support the claim; right angles between walls that were still fluid, or 120-degree meetings against already rigid walls, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Time-resolved meristem volumes from which successive walls and their meeting angles can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Fixed embryo volumes spanning successive divisions, for angle statistics where wall age can be inferred from the lineage

obstacles: Wall rigidity is usually inferred from age or cellulose signal rather than measured directly in these stacks.
Coverage is concentrated on Arabidopsis, not plant tissues at large.
rationale: The angle prediction is sharp, and meristem and embryo volumes contain the walls. What they lack for a full test is a direct marker that the older wall had solidified before the new one arrived. Angle-versus-sequence comparisons are feasible for Arabidopsis and remain a proxy for the rigidity mechanism across plants.

operationalization: In filamentous cyanobacteria and similar pairs, class partition curvature as flat, hemispheric or more than hemispheric and, where possible, compare that class with measured tension at the outer surface and at the cell-cell boundary. The three shape classes tracking the three tension regimes would support the claim; shapes that stay flat across independently varied boundary tension would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public micrographs of filamentous and paired cells from which partition curvature can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Additional annotated light and electron micrographs of simple cell chains

obstacles: Under a soap-film model the curvature is the tension ratio, so shape classes alone restate the claim.
Independent tension measurements in Nostoc and its allies are not part of these image archives.
rationale: Photographs can sort paired cells into the three curvature classes the claim names. They cannot supply the two tensions those classes are said to express, and treating curvature as a tension measurement makes the test circular. The shape catalogue is therefore only a partial check.

operationalization: In three-dimensional segmentations of parenchyma, epithelia and early embryos, measure the angles at which walls meet and the curvature of walls between cells of different sizes. Triple junctions near 120 degrees regardless of cell size, with curvature set by the size difference, would support the claim; common four-way junctions, angles far from 120 degrees, or curvature unrelated to neighbouring sizes would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Expert 3D segmentations of meristem cells for triple-junction angles and neighbour-size effects on wall curvature

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-wall-stained embryo volumes spanning many cell sizes in one aggregate

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Animal epithelial and other tissue volumes for the same angle and curvature measurements outside plants

obstacles: Anisotropic stress and recent divisions are known to pull some junctions off 120 degrees, so the test needs a pre-registered exclusion or a report of that bias.
Honeycomb and every plant parenchyma type are not in these three collections.
rationale: Triple-junction angle and wall curvature are standard measurements on segmentations that can already be downloaded. The prediction that angle is independent of cell size while curvature is not is distinguishable from right-angle or random-junction alternatives. A small team can run that test on meristems, embryos and public epithelia with existing tools.

operationalization: In four-cell embryos whose blastomeres are in full contact, score whether a polar furrow is present or the four cells meet at one point. A short intermediate partition in essentially every such embryo would support the claim; stable four-way crosses in fully apposed fluid blastomeres would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Public Xenopus developmental images, including cleavage stages at which the four-cell contact can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
candidate_datasets.role: Sea-urchin developmental images and associated resources for early cleavage geometry

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable embryo image and quantitative-dynamics sets for remeasuring four-cell contacts in three dimensions

obstacles: A cross seen in a single optical plane can hide a short polar furrow, so only 3D or time-resolved volumes are decisive.
Molluscs and annelids, classical material for this stage, are less completely archived than frog and sea urchin.
rationale: Presence or absence of a polar furrow is a yes-or-no observation, and public cleavage images of frog, sea urchin and other embryos are sufficient to make it. Three-dimensional sets remove the viewing-angle error the claim says produced reports of a simple cross. Coverage is uneven across phyla, but it is enough to confirm or refute the pattern in eggs whose blastomeres meet in full contact.

operationalization: Measure the external contact angle of neighbouring blastomeres and, separately, the tensions at cell-cell and cell-medium surfaces. External angles below 120 degrees where cell-cell tension exceeds either cell-medium tension, and point contact where cell-cell tension reaches the sum of the other two, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Cleavage images showing rounded versus closely apposed blastomeres

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative embryo image sets from which contact angles and intercellular spaces can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
candidate_datasets.role: Sea-urchin cleavage material for the same contact geometry

obstacles: Contact angle defines the tension ratio if Young's law is assumed, so geometry alone does not independently test the tensions.
Eggshells and extracellular coats can hold blastomeres apart and mimic point contact.
rationale: Rounded blastomeres and the angles of their contacts are measurable in existing embryo volumes. The claim's content is a tension inequality, and these archives do not contain the tensions. The geometric catalogue can be checked, while the force law remains confounded with extracellular constraints.

operationalization: Compare outer-layer cells with interior cells for flattening, rectangular outline and near-right angles at the outer wall, and ask whether those traits track position alone. Outer cells showing that suite because they lie outside, including after identity programs are perturbed, would support the claim; an epidermal shape program that appears independent of outside position would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Early embryo volumes in which the outer cell layer can be compared with interior cells

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented meristems with an outer layer whose angles and aspect ratios are measurable

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Further plant and animal tissue volumes with a distinguished outer layer

obstacles: Position and epidermal identity are usually confounded, and these geometry sets do not include the identity-perturbation experiments.
Laminaria-type simple thalli are not in the Arabidopsis-heavy archives.
rationale: Outer versus inner cell shape is directly measurable in open embryo and meristem segmentations, so the positional pattern can be tested. The claim also says the physical features follow from that position through unequal, consolidated tensions, which the images do not measure. Identity programs remain a live alternative for the same flattened outer layer.

operationalization: Relate polygon regularity, such as variation in side length and angle, to cell-size variation and to directional stretch in surface epithelia and parenchyma. Regular hexagons restricted to regions of uniform cell size and no directional traction, with irregular or elongated polygons where size varies or growth is anisotropic, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented meristem surfaces where cell-size variation and polygon regularity can be compared locally

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Epithelial image volumes, including tissues with more uniform cells, for the same regularity statistics

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional comb reconstructions of similar-sized hexagonal cells as a uniform-size comparison

obstacles: Retinal pigment epithelium, Thompson's showcase of regular hexagons, is not a tabulated layer in these sets and would have to be added from other public images.
Average side number near six is expected from topology alone, so the test has to use regularity, not merely the mean.
rationale: Regularity against cell-size variation is a direct morphometric comparison, and segmented meristems already contain both variables, including local contrasts between equal and unequal cells. Epithelial volumes and uniform comb cells extend the comparison. The named retinal epithelium is a gap in coverage, not a gap in method, and the outcome would still favour or count against the stated size rule.

operationalization: Wherever similar cylinders or spheres are in complete surface contact, measure neighbour number and junction angle in section or surface view, and compare them with loose bundles that do not touch along faces. Complete contact yielding hexagons with angles near 120 degrees, and incomplete contact leaving round profiles, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Close-packed meristem cells for neighbour counts and junction angles

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional bee comb, a close-packed hexagonal prism system in the claim's scope

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D scans of colonial corals and other packed biological bodies for contact versus cylindrical outlines

obstacles: Any trivalent tiling averages six sides, so neighbour number alone is a weak discriminator and angle plus completeness of contact have to carry the test.
Scans and segmentations over-represent model plants, honeybees and a few coral colonies.
rationale: The packing prediction can be scored with neighbour counts and angles on data that already exist for epithelia, comb and corals. The informative contrast is complete facial contact versus cylinders that only touch locally. That comparison is standard image analysis and is sufficient to confirm or refute the stated tendency, with the topological average kept in view as a bias.

operationalization: Count corallite sides in massive colonies whose polyps are in contact and compare the mean and the spread with fasciculate colonies whose corallites stay free. Close-packed colonies with a mean near six sides, more spread where sizes vary, and cylindrical corallites where contact is loose, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable 3D scans of colonial coral skeletons from which corallite outlines and contacts can be counted

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Aggregated museum images of fossil and living corals, including massive and fasciculate colony forms

candidate_datasets.name: Coral Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Open trait tables of colony growth form and calyx morphology for separating close-packed from loosely branched species

obstacles: Side number is not a column in the trait database and has to be counted from images and scans.
Paleozoic genera named by Thompson are photographed less evenly than living massive corals, and abrasion can round corners.
rationale: Mean side number under close contact, versus cylindrical outlines when corallites are free, is a direct count on public specimen images and scans. Colony growth form is already tabulated and sorts the two habits. Counting a broad sample is weeks of ordinary morphometry, enough to resolve the packing claim for massive versus fasciculate colonies.

operationalization: On three-dimensional reconstructions of hive-bee comb, measure the prism angles in plan and the angles of the three rhombs that close the cell. Prism angles near 120 degrees and a trihedral angle near 109.5 degrees would support the rhombic-dodecahedron description; a flat or differently angled base would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: X-ray volumes and reconstructions of Apis mellifera comb from which prism and, where the base is in frame, rhomb angles can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: Natural comb cell-orientation measurements
candidate_datasets.role: Measured in-plane orientations of hexagonal cells in natural Apis mellifera and Apis cerana combs

obstacles: The released tables report cell size and tilt, so the rhombic-cap angle has to be measured from the volumes rather than read off a column.
Much of the X-ray material was built on experimental foundations, which may alter the base relative to natural comb.
rationale: The claim is a specific geometric description of one structure, the hive-bee cell, and open X-ray volumes of that structure exist. Prism geometry is already implicit in the hexagonal segmentations, and the diagnostic cap angle is measurable if the cell base was scanned. The foundation-comb caveat lowers adequacy without removing the possibility of a direct test.

operationalization: Combine comb geometry with construction sequences: test whether walls flow to the rhombic and hexagonal configuration while wax or pulp is semi-fluid and the insects only extrude close-packed tubes. Automatic attainment of the angles in bee-free semi-fluid wax would support the claim; active sculpting of the angles, or geometry that appears only where bees work the wall, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Honeycomb X-ray microscopy
candidate_datasets.role: Three-dimensional records of how Apis mellifera changes cell geometry when the starting foundation size is altered, evidence about construction behaviour

obstacles: Finished angles are compatible with surface tension, with thermoplastic flow, and with behavioural building, so outcome geometry does not identify the agency.
Wasp paper comb and direct wax-temperature or surface-tension measurements are not in this honeybee deposit.
rationale: Public three-dimensional comb data show bees merging, tilting and layering cells as foundation size changes, which speaks to an active building process. They do not record wax fluidity or surface tension during wall formation, so the proposed automatic mechanism is only indirectly constrained. The rival of deliberate wax economy is likewise only partly addressed.

operationalization: Count faces and face shapes of interior cells in symmetrical, near-equal parenchyma. A mode near twelve rhombic faces would support the dodecahedral claim; a mode near fourteen with hexagonal and square faces would support Kelvin's tetrakaidecahedron instead.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: 3D cell segmentations from which face number and neighbour counts of interior cells can be computed

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo volumes whose interior cells can be segmented for the same face census

obstacles: Meristem and embryo cells are a young, growing subset of the symmetrical parenchyma the claim is about.
Surface cells must be excluded, because the twelve-versus-fourteen contrast is about interior cells of a bulk foam.
rationale: Face number is a clean discriminator between the rhombic dodecahedron and Kelvin's fourteen-sided cell, and public segmentations make the count feasible. Those segmentations are meristems and early embryos rather than mature equal-celled parenchyma such as pith. The ideal can be tested in a restricted tissue class and not yet across the stated scope.

operationalization: Ask whether late-cleavage geometry continues to satisfy the same minimal-surface and contact rules that fix the two- and four-cell stages, with no extra lineage-specific parameters. Late embryos whose contacts and angles match a surface-mechanics extrapolation would support that reading; stereotyped positions that violate those constraints would limit it.

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative image series of later cleavage in several animals

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Frog cleavage images past the four-cell stage

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
candidate_datasets.role: Sea-urchin embryos at advancing cleavage stages

obstacles: Simple physical laws can be stretched to cover almost any material configuration, so the decision rule needs a pre-specified constraint set.
Fitting a full mechanical model of advanced cleavage is specialist work and is longer than a routine remeasurement.
rationale: Late-cleavage images are public and can be checked against the Plateau-type constraints developed for early stages, which is a fair partial reading of the claim. The assertion that the whole configuration is accurately determined by simple physical laws does not name which laws, and many outcomes fit both those laws and lineage-specific developmental programs. Only the restricted geometric continuation is testable now.

operationalization: At the four-cell stage, predict polar-furrow arrangement from relative blastomere volumes and compare that prediction with a model that assigns arrangements by clade. Arrangements tracking size ratios, with little phylogenetic signal once size is controlled, would support the claim; clade-conserved furrows at the same size ratios would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Frog four-cell images for furrow class and relative blastomere size

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
candidate_datasets.role: Sea-urchin cleavage images as a second phylum for the same comparison

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative early-embryo sets in which cell volumes and contact topology can be measured together

obstacles: Molluscs, annelids and coelenterates, where many of the classical furrow variants were drawn, are poorly represented in these databases.
Related species often share egg proportions, so size and classification are not fully independent.
rationale: Relative cell size versus furrow topology is a well-posed comparison, and it can be started on frog and sea-urchin volumes. The claim's scope is a cross-phylum distribution, and most of that comparative sample is still in uncompiled embryological plates. Phylogenetic non-independence of egg size is a real but manageable confound for the subset that is digitized.

operationalization: The claim asserts that no stage of development shows physical forces giving way to agencies outside physics. Any unexplained embryonic pattern is compatible both with physics not yet identified and with a vital agency, so no public measurement distinguishes the two.
obstacles: An agency unknown to physics has no separate observable that a dataset could record.
Failure to find a non-physical residue is not a confirming result under this wording.
rationale: This is a conceptual denial that vital agencies replace physical ones, not a statement with a measurable residue. Developmental image archives contain forms and genes and forces, and none of those variables marks the boundary the claim denies. Every empirical outcome can be read as still physical, so the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted by existing data.

operationalization: Among cells that are roughly rectangular and divide into near-equal daughters, test whether the new wall cuts the longest axis and whether the next wall is perpendicular to the previous one. That pattern would support the claim; equal divisions parallel to the long axis, or successive walls that are not orthogonal, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: 3D wall-stained embryos for division-plane orientation against mother-cell axes

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented meristem cells with successive division orientations

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Further plant cell-division volumes for oblong cells outside the embryo and meristem

obstacles: Many cells in these volumes are not rectangular, so the test has to be restricted to the shape the rule assumes.
Tissue stress orients some divisions and can mimic or mask a pure longest-axis rule.
rationale: The longest-axis rule and the right-angle alternation are explicit and apply to a recognizable subset of cells in public embryo and meristem volumes. Standard geometric measurements can confirm or refute them for that subset within weeks. Adequacy is limited to model plants rather than rectangular dividing cells in general, which is still enough for the rule as a biological regularity.

operationalization: For symmetric divisions, compare the area of the observed partition with the least area that can divide the mother-cell volume, and with plausible larger alternatives such as a fixed genetic plane. Observed walls clustering on the area minimum would support Errera's rule; a systematic preference for a larger surface would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo volumes already used to compare observed division surfaces with geometric rules, including area minimization

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Meristem segmentations for the same area comparison in a growing tissue

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Additional public division-plane image sets beyond Arabidopsis embryos

obstacles: Several geometric rules nearly coincide in symmetric cells, so the test needs asymmetric and irregular mothers where the minimum is unique.
Computing a minimal surface is specialist but is an established method in this literature.
rationale: Errera's least-area rule is a direct comparison between an observed wall and a computable surface, and open embryo and meristem segmentations contain both the volumes and the walls. That comparison has already been framed on data of this kind and can be repeated or extended with current tools. Overlap with other geometric rules is a known bias and is reducible by choosing cells where the candidate surfaces differ.

operationalization: For unequal divisions of roughly cubical cells, plot partition shape against the volume fraction cut off. Curved corner walls below about three-tenths, and spherical octants below about 0.15, with plane walls above the threshold, would support the claim; plane walls remaining common below three-tenths would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo volumes that include unequal divisions whose volume fraction and wall curvature can be measured as a partial analogue

obstacles: Fucus hairs, moss paraphyses and stomatal precursors, the cases named for this corner geometry, are not in the embryo collection.
Two-dimensional sections underestimate the difference between a quarter-cylinder and a plane.
rationale: The volume thresholds are numerically explicit, so the pattern would be decisive if cubical cells with known daughter volumes were archived. Public embryo volumes offer some unequal divisions and not the corner-cutting geometry of the named hairs and precursors. The rule can be probed on a proxy tissue and cannot yet be resolved for the cells it was stated about.

operationalization: On quadrant-shaped flat cells, measure where the anticlinal wall meets the straight sides and what angle of arc it cuts off. An arc that meets both edges at right angles, cuts off about 55 degrees, and starts near three-tenths of the radius would support the claim; a straight radial wall or a periclinal wall in equal halves would refute it.
obstacles: Erythrotrichia discs and pressure-flattened frog or sea-urchin eggs are illustrated in classical plates, not in a public coordinate table.
The numerical arc and radius fractions need measured outlines rather than schematic drawings.
rationale: The predicted arc is specific enough that a modest set of quadrant cells would confirm or refute it. Those cells are not available as an open morphometric dataset, though published figures show the qualitative anticlinal curve. The quantitative constants are only partly checkable from existing images.

operationalization: Measure the apical angle of sector-shaped cells and whether the next wall is anticlinal or periclinal. Anticlinal walls concentrated between about 62.5 and 90 degrees, and periclinal walls in narrower sectors, would support the claim; anticlinal walls common in narrow sectors would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Segmented shoot apices in which wedge-shaped cells and the orientation of the next wall can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Embryo cells with sector-like outlines for the same angle-versus-orientation test

obstacles: Meristem surface cells are polygonal prisms more often than the flat circular sectors the threshold was derived for.
Flattened discs and fern apices in the stated scope are mostly uncompiled.
rationale: The angular window is a sharp, refutable prediction, and some wedge-shaped cells in public apex and embryo volumes can be scored for wall orientation. Those cells are an imperfect match to the circular-sector geometry used to derive 62.5 degrees. The test is informative for growing points that have been segmented and incomplete for the wider scope.

operationalization: Follow a uniformly growing flat disc after a quadrant divides into a triangular and a quadrilateral daughter, and record which daughter divides next and at what radius. The triangular cell reaching division size first, near 1.35 times the starting radius against about 1.52 for the quadrilateral, would support the claim; simultaneous division, or the quadrilateral dividing first, would refute it.
obstacles: No public time-lapse of Erythrotrichia or a similar disc records daughter area against disc radius through the next division.
Fixed embryo collections cannot supply the division-time order this numerical prediction requires.
rationale: The claim predicts both an order of division and two radius ratios under uniform disc growth. That is a clean test and it needs live, cell-resolved growth of that geometry. Such a series is not in current open datasets, so the constants cannot be confirmed or refuted without new observations.

operationalization: In discoid embryos, algal discs and antheridia, test whether repeated divisions leave a peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells with radial walls, and whether a minimal-area division sequence reproduces that layer. A peripheral quadrilateral epidermis generated by that sequence would support the claim; a peripheral layer whose divisions do not follow the minimal-area order would weaken the proposed origin.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Early embryo volumes in which a peripheral cell layer and its division orientations can be inspected

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Additional public images of embryonic and thalloid surfaces with an outer cell layer

obstacles: A quadrilateral epidermis can be produced by an identity program as well as by successive least-area divisions.
Moss embryos, algal discs and antheridia are sparsely represented next to Arabidopsis.
rationale: The finished pattern, a superficial file of parallel-sided cells, is visible in some open embryo volumes. Showing that the pattern is the residue of minimal-area divisions needs the division sequence or a model comparison tied to those cells. Existing data can check the pattern in a few systems and only partly test the proposed mechanism.

operationalization: Classify the surface partition pattern of many eight-cell frog eggs and test whether more than one topological type occurs at appreciable frequency. Several recurring arrangements within the species would support the claim; a single arrangement in nearly every egg would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Xenopus image resources covering early cleavage, from which eight-cell surface patterns can be classified

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Quantitative embryo datasets that include individually resolved cleavage stages

obstacles: Atlas images preferentially show a textbook arrangement, which is the sampling bias the claim is warning against.
A frequency count needs many individual eggs, and public atlases are not already tabulated that way.
rationale: Within-species variability of the eight-cell pattern is a direct frequency question, and frog cleavage images are public. They are not a random sample of eggs with arrangements already scored, so a small team would still be compiling rather than downloading a finished census. The test is well posed and only partly executable on what is archived.

operationalization: Classify surface eight-cell groups, animal and plant, into the thirteen topological types implied by three-way meetings and no submerged cell, and count exceptions. Every group that meets those premises falling into one of the thirteen types would support the empirical rider; a recurring surface arrangement that meets the premises and fits none of the types would refute the enumeration.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Frog eight-cell images for typing surface partitions

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Plant embryos at stages with a small number of surface cells

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
candidate_datasets.role: Sea-urchin cleavage images as a further animal sample

obstacles: If the three-way and all-cells-on-the-surface premises hold, the thirteen types are a combinatorial list, and images cannot reveal a fourteenth type without breaking a premise.
Many real eight-cell groups include an internal cell or a transient four-way junction and so sit outside the claim's antecedent.
rationale: The enumeration is largely a theorem about partitions, and datasets test only whether real surface groups obey its premises and look like the listed types. Public cleavage and embryo images support that conformity check for a few organisms. They do not convert the combinatorial statement into an independent empirical law, which limits both discriminating power and scope.

operationalization: Rank eight-cell and similar small aggregates by how evenly contacts are distributed among the cells, and compare that rank with how often each arrangement occurs. Frequency falling as contact variance rises would support the claim; common arrangements in which one cell takes most of the contacts would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Cleavage images from which contact counts per blastomere can be tallied

candidate_datasets.name: SSBD
candidate_datasets.role: Individual embryo volumes suitable for contact graphs of small cell groups

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Plant embryos for the same evenness-versus-frequency comparison

obstacles: Published figures over-sample arrangements authors considered normal, which can fake a stability ranking.
Oil-drop models mentioned alongside cells are not part of these biological archives.
rationale: Evenness of contacts and the frequency of each arrangement are both countable from cleavage volumes, and their correlation is a real prediction. The volumes are not a balanced sample across the types, and frequencies have not been deposited. A biased atlas can support a partial test and cannot yet establish which arrangements are the commonest in nature.

operationalization: Assemble partition topologies of small cell groups and of small organs across plants and animals, and test whether the same few graphs recur with weak phylogenetic signal. The same configurations in distant lineages, and relatedness adding little once topology is constrained, would support the claim; configurations clustering by clade would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Xenbase
candidate_datasets.role: Vertebrate early-embryo partitions for cross-group comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Plant embryo partitions as the botanical side of the same comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Echinobase
candidate_datasets.role: Echinoderm cleavage as a third lineage

obstacles: If only a few topologies are possible, recurrence is expected and does not by itself explain why those topologies were used.
Organs, as opposed to early cell groups, are not coded as partition graphs in these databases.
rationale: A three-lineage sample of early embryos can show whether a few cell-partition types are shared. That is a fragment of a claim that also covers organs and the whole of plants and animals, most of which is uncompiled. Shared topology is only weakly discriminating once the number of legal partitions is already small.

operationalization: Compare fossula geometry in rugose corals with the septal graphs expected from three-way meetings, and test whether fossulae co-vary with other bilateral organ systems. Fossulae that match packing variants and occur without a broader bilateral suite would support the space-partition reading; fossulae aligned with a conserved bilateral plane and other bilateral traits would leave the higher-organization reading standing.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of coral skeletons, some of which resolve septal contacts

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Museum photographs of Heterophyllia, Zaphrentis and other rugose corals

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence and taxonomic data for placing fossulate corals in a phylogenetic and stratigraphic sample

obstacles: Showing that a fossula is a legal three-way packing does not rule out a biological bilateral function for the same chamber.
Septal junctions are often obscured in photographs of abraded fossils, and side-by-side organ-grade characters are not coded for these genera.
rationale: Specimen images and scans can test whether fossulae look like ordinary completions of a trivalent septal network. The claim's denial that this indicates a higher bilateral grade is an inference about how the structure should be read, and packing compatibility does not uniquely decide it. Occurrence data help with sampling and do not supply the morphological test by themselves.

operationalization: Measure epidermal cell aspect ratio and the spatial arrangement of stomata on the same leaves. Stomata in rows where cells are oblong, and irregularly placed where cells are polygonal, including within lineages that break the monocot-dicot pairing, would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis stomatal coordinates
candidate_datasets.role: Pixel coordinates of every stomate on 66 Arabidopsis leaves, for testing whether stomata on a polygonal epidermis are scattered rather than rowed

obstacles: The open coordinate table is Arabidopsis, a polygonal case, and does not include the oblong-celled monocot leaves that should show rows.
Monocots tend to have both oblong cells and stomatal files, so phylogeny and cell shape have to be separated.
rationale: Row versus scattered arrangement against cell shape is a clear spatial test, and one half of it, scattered stomata on a polygonal epidermis, can be measured from a deposited coordinate table. The oblong-cell, rowed half is widely illustrated and not similarly compiled. Phylogenetic confounding between grasses and files keeps even a future two-sided test from being automatic.

operationalization: Compare mature pollen and spore shape with whether the wall rigidified before the tetrad separated. Grains that hardened in the tetrad keeping plane facets and sharp angles, and grains that separated while soft becoming spherical, would support the claim; spherical grains that hardened in permanent tetrads, or angular grains that separated soft, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PalDat
candidate_datasets.role: Public pollen micrographs and shape descriptors, including pollen-unit type, for scoring spherical versus faceted grains and tetrad retention

obstacles: PalDat records shape and whether grains are united, not the developmental timing of wall hardening relative to separation.
Apertures, harmomegathy and drying also produce facets, and fern and red-algal spores are outside this pollen database.
rationale: Pollen shape and tetrad versus monad status are openly coded for a large angiosperm sample, which proxies the claim by asking whether retained tetrads are the faceted grains. The actual timing of solidification is in scattered ultrastructural studies, not in PalDat. Shape has several other causes, so the association is informative and confounded.

operationalization: At cryptogam apices, compare the frequency of buds and other outgrowths on triangular cells with the frequency on quadrangular cells, holding position on the apex constant. A higher outgrowth rate on triangular cells would support the claim; no bias, or a bias toward quadrangular cells, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public confocal sets that include some bryophyte apices where superficial cell shape and branch sites can be scored

obstacles: Triangular cells often sit at the tip, so shape and the position where buds arise are collinear unless position is controlled.
Moss, liverwort, fern and algal apices are not gathered in one shape-by-outgrowth table.
rationale: A preference for outgrowths on triangular cells is a countable bias, and some apical images exist to start the count. Coverage of cryptogams is thin, and the classical anatomical plates are not a clean sample. Position is a serious confound because the cells the claim singles out also occupy the usual bud site.

operationalization: Record cell shape immediately before division and the plane that is used: transverse in markedly oblong cells, oblique when the cell is a little more than a hemisphere, and longitudinal when it is less than a hemisphere. That mapping, in cells whose shape was set by the growth-to-division interval, would support the claim; planes uncorrelated with those shape classes would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis embryo image collection
candidate_datasets.role: Mother-cell shapes and daughter walls for a proxy test of the shape-to-plane map

candidate_datasets.name: Arabidopsis shoot-meristem segmentations
candidate_datasets.role: Meristem cells with geometry just before and after division

obstacles: Shape is partly defined by the growth-to-division ratio, so that half of the wording is close to a description of the cell that is about to divide.
The three-way rule was stated for moss, liverwort, fern and algal apical cells, which these Arabidopsis volumes only approximate.
rationale: The shape-to-plane mapping is measurable and overlaps rules that public embryo and meristem volumes were built to study. Those volumes are the wrong taxa for the apical cells named in the claim, so they test a proxy. The growth-rate clause adds little beyond the shape already observed, which caps how decisive a confirmation can be.
